steps: Clean the fish thoroughly and pat it dry, then score the skin diagonally a few times on each side so the marinade can penetrate and the skin crisps evenly.
Blend the spice paste ingredients (turmeric, chili, garlic, ginger) into a smooth paste, adding a splash of oil if it needs loosening.
Stir in half the lime juice and the sliced chili to brighten the paste before it goes on the fish.
Rub the paste all over the fish, inside and out, working it into the scored cuts, then season generously with salt and pepper.
Cover and let the fish marinate for at least 30 minutes at room temperature, or up to 2 hours in the fridge for deeper flavor.
Preheat the grill to medium-high heat and oil the grates well so the skin doesn't stick and tear.
Place the fish on the grill and cook for 6-8 minutes per side, basting with oil every couple of minutes.
Turn carefully once the skin releases easily from the grates, the fish is done when the flesh flakes easily and the skin is charred in spots.
Rest for a few minutes off the heat, then finish with the remaining lime juice and a scatter of fresh chili before serving.
Bring the steaks to room temperature for about 20 minutes before cooking so they sear evenly.
Mince the garlic and rub it all over both sides of the steaks along with a generous seasoning of salt and pepper.
Tuck a few sprigs of rosemary or thyme against the meat, drizzle with oil, and work it in, then cover and marinate for at least an hour, longer develops more flavor.
Light the braai and let the coals burn down until they're covered in white ash and radiating steady heat.
Place the steaks over the hottest part of the fire and sear for 2-3 minutes per side without moving them, to build a good crust.
Move to slightly cooler coals and continue grilling to your preferred doneness, turning once more.
While the steaks rest, grill the onion rings over the coals for 3-4 minutes per side until softened and lightly charred.
Use a meat thermometer or the touch test to check doneness, about 54C for medium-rare.
Rest the steaks on a board for at least 5 minutes before slicing, then serve topped with the grilled onions and fresh herbs.
Slice the onion and mince the garlic.
Season the chicken pieces generously with salt and pepper on all sides.
Heat oil in a heavy pot and saute the onion until soft, then add the garlic and cook until fragrant, about a minute.
Add the chicken pieces and brown them lightly on all sides, about 5 minutes, this is about building flavor, not cooking through yet.
Tuck the fresh thyme or curry leaves in among the chicken so their fragrance infuses as it cooks.
Pour in the coconut milk, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom of the pot.
Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce the heat to low and cover.
Simmer for 30-35 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is tender and cooked through.
Uncover for the last 5-10 minutes if the sauce needs to thicken further, then taste and adjust the seasoning before serving.
Whisk the spice blend together with the coconut milk, oil, and half the lime juice until well combined into a fragrant marinade.
Season the chicken pieces with salt and pepper, then add them to the marinade and turn to coat every surface evenly.
Cover and let the chicken marinate for at least 20 minutes, or up to a few hours in the fridge for deeper flavor.
Preheat the grill to medium heat, too hot and the coconut milk marinade will scorch before the chicken cooks through.
Lift the chicken from the marinade, letting the excess drip off, and reserve the marinade for basting.
Grill the chicken pieces, turning every few minutes and basting with the reserved marinade each time you flip.
Continue grilling for about 20-25 minutes total, until the outside is golden and slightly charred.
Check that the chicken is cooked through, juices run clear, no pink near the bone.
Rest briefly, then squeeze the remaining lime juice over the top before serving hot.
Pat the goat chunks dry and season generously with salt and pepper.
Heat oil in a heavy pot and fry the curry spice blend and minced garlic together for about a minute, until fragrant.
Add the chopped onion and cook until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes.
Add the goat and brown it on all sides, turning occasionally, for about 8-10 minutes.
Stir in the chopped tomatoes and cook for a few minutes until they start to soften and release their juices.
Add enough water to just cover the meat, then bring to a boil.
Reduce the heat to low, cover, and simmer gently for about 75-90 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the fresh thyme or curry leaves partway through cooking so their flavor infuses the sauce.
Check the goat for tenderness, it should pull apart easily with a fork, then uncover for the last 10-15 minutes to reduce and thicken the sauce before serving.
Combine the lime juice, sliced onions, oil, chili, minced garlic, salt, and pepper in a large bowl or bag.
Add the chicken pieces and turn to coat thoroughly in the marinade.
Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 2 hours, turning occasionally, the lime juice does most of the flavor work here.
Lift the chicken from the marinade, shaking off the excess, and set the marinated onions aside separately.
Grill or pan-fry the chicken over medium-high heat until browned on all sides, about 10-12 minutes, it doesn't need to be fully cooked through yet.
In a separate pan, fry the reserved onions over medium heat, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 15 minutes.
Return the browned chicken to the pan with the onions and pour in the reserved marinade.
Cover and simmer gently for 20-25 minutes, until the chicken is tender and cooked through and the onions have melted into a soft, tangy sauce.
Taste and adjust the seasoning with more salt or lime juice, then scatter with chopped parsley before serving.
Combine the jerk spice blend, scotch bonnet chili, minced garlic, and fresh thyme in a mortar or food processor and grind into a coarse, fragrant paste.
Stir the lime juice and oil into the paste until it forms a thick, spreadable marinade, then season it with salt and pepper.
Score the chicken pieces lightly and rub the marinade all over, working it under the skin where you can for maximum flavor.
Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least an hour, overnight develops the best, deepest flavor.
Bring the chicken to room temperature for 20-30 minutes before grilling.
Preheat the grill to medium heat and set it up for indirect cooking if possible, since jerk chicken benefits from a slower cook.
Grill the chicken, turning often to keep the sugars in the marinade from burning, for about 30-35 minutes total.
In the final few minutes, move the chicken over direct heat briefly to build a deep char on the skin.
Check that the chicken is cooked through before serving hot, ideally with extra lime wedges on the side.
Chop the tomatoes, onion, and chili finely, and mince the garlic, keeping them separate for now.
Season the fish lightly with salt and pat it dry so it sears rather than steams.
Heat oil in a wide pan and sear the fish pieces briefly on each side just to color the outside, then set aside.
In the same pan, saute the onion until soft and translucent, then add the garlic and cook until fragrant.
Stir in the spice blend and cook for about 30 seconds until fragrant, then add the tomatoes and chili.
Cook the tomatoes down, stirring occasionally, until they break apart into a thick sauce.
Season the sauce with salt and a splash of water if it looks too thick, then let it simmer for a few minutes to meld the flavors.
Nestle the seared fish back into the sauce, spooning some sauce over the top.
Cover and simmer gently for 8-10 minutes, until the fish is opaque and flakes easily and the sauce has thickened to your liking.
Grind the berbere spice blend together with the chili, garlic, and a splash of oil into a thick, fragrant awaze paste.
Season the beef cubes with salt and pepper.
Chop the onion, tomatoes, and rosemary, keeping them ready near the stove.
Heat the remaining oil in a wide pan or skillet over high heat until it's just starting to smoke.
Sear the beef cubes in batches, turning occasionally, until well browned on all sides but still rare in the center, about 4-5 minutes per batch.
Push the beef to one side, add the onion to the pan, and fry until it softens and picks up the browned bits, about 3-4 minutes.
Stir in the awaze paste and tomatoes, tossing everything together until the beef is evenly coated and glossy.
Cook for a final 2-3 minutes so the sauce clings and thickens slightly without overcooking the beef.
Finish with the lime juice and rosemary, tossing once more, then serve hot straight from the pan.
Finely chop the onions, mince the garlic, and chop the tomatoes.
Pat the lamb dry and season generously with salt and pepper.
Heat the oil (or butter) in a heavy pot and cook the onions over medium-low heat until soft and translucent, about 10 minutes, take it slow, alicha wot is a mild, gently built stew.
Add the garlic and mild spice blend and cook for another minute until fragrant, being careful not to let it brown or turn bitter.
Add the lamb and turn it in the spiced onions until lightly coated, about 3-4 minutes, no need for a deep sear here.
Stir in the tomatoes and cook for a few minutes until they soften and begin to break down.
Pour in the coconut milk and enough water to almost cover the lamb, then bring to a gentle simmer.
Cover and simmer on low for 60-70 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lamb is fork-tender.
Uncover, add the fresh rosemary and lime juice, and simmer a final 5 minutes to let the sauce settle before serving.
Slice the beef into thin strips against the grain so they stay tender when seared quickly.
Slice the onion, chili, and tomatoes into matching strips and wedges, and mince the garlic.
Season the beef strips with salt, pepper, and the berbere spice blend.
Heat the oil in a heavy skillet or on a hot grill plate until very hot.
Sear the beef strips in a single layer, in batches if needed, for about 1-2 minutes per side, zilzil tibs is meant to be quick and hot, not slow-cooked.
Remove the beef and set aside, then add the onion and garlic to the same pan and fry for 2-3 minutes until just softened.
Add the chili and tomatoes and cook for another minute, tossing to pick up the fond left by the beef.
Return the beef to the pan along with the rosemary, tossing everything together over high heat for a final minute.
Finish with a squeeze of lime juice and serve immediately while sizzling hot.
Grind the jerk spice blend together with the garlic, chili, and thyme into a coarse, oily paste.
Pat the pork chops dry, season with salt and pepper, then rub the spice paste all over, working it into the bone pockets.
Stir the lime juice into any remaining paste and drizzle it over the chops.
Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 1-2 hours, or overnight for the best flavor.
Bring the chops to room temperature for 20 minutes before grilling.
Preheat the grill to medium-high heat and oil the grates well.
Grill the chops for 5-6 minutes per side, until well charred and an internal temperature of about 63C near the bone.
While the chops rest, quickly toss the sliced onion and chopped tomatoes on the grill or in a hot pan for 2-3 minutes to soften into a warm relish.
Rest the chops for 5 minutes, then serve topped with the onion-tomato relish and a final squeeze of lime.
